statement: Challenger mission 51-L began its flight at 11:38 a.m. EST on 28 January 1986.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: Flight of the Space Shuttle Challenger on Mission 51-L began at 11:38 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on January 28, 1986.
timeBasis: Source gives Eastern Standard Time (EST = UTC-5); converted to UTC. The event table gives SRM ignition command (T=0) at 16:38:00.010 GMT.

statement: The flight ended 73 seconds after launch in an explosive burn of hydrogen and oxygen propellants that destroyed the External Tank; aerodynamic loads caused complete structural breakup of the Orbiter and all seven crew members perished.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: It ended 73 seconds later in an explosive burn of hydrogen and oxygen propellants that destroyed the External Tank and exposed the Orbiter to severe aerodynamic loads that caused complete structural breakup. All seven crew members perished.

statement: SRM ignition command (T=0) occurred at 16:38:00.010 GMT per General Purpose Computer data.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, pp. 37-39, table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events", row "SRM Ignition Command (T=O)"
excerpt: 38:00.010 SRM Ignition Command (T=O) 0.000 GPC
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC.

statement: Ambient air temperature at launch was 36 degrees F, measured at ground level about 1,000 feet from pad 39B, 15 degrees colder than any previous launch.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: The ambient air temperature at launch was 36 degrees Fahrenheit measured at ground level approximately 1,000 feet from the 51-L mission launch pad 39B. This temperature was 15 degrees colder than that of any previous launch.

statement: At 0.678 s MET, photographic data show a strong puff of gray smoke from the vicinity of the right SRB aft field joint (E60 camera; 16:38:00.688 GMT).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19; event table row "Confirmed smoke above field joint on RH SRM"
excerpt: Just after liftoff at .678 seconds into the flight, photographic data show a strong puff of gray smoke was spurting from the vicinity of the aft field joint on the right Solid Rocket Booster.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 0.678 s.

statement: Computer graphic analysis placed the initial smoke in the 270- to 310-degree sector of the right SRB aft field joint circumference, the side facing the External Tank; the pad 39B cameras that would have recorded the precise location were inoperative.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: Computer graphic analysis of film from other cameras indicated the initial smoke came from the 270 to 310-degree sector of the circumference of the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Booster. This area of the solid booster faces the External Tank.

statement: Eight more puffs of increasingly blacker smoke were recorded between 0.836 and 2.500 s MET.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: Eight more distinctive puffs of increasingly blacker smoke were recorded between .836 and 2.500 seconds.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. Time is the first of the eight puffs (MET 0.836 s).

statement: The first very small flame on the right SRB near the aft field joint was detected on image-enhanced film at 58.788 s MET (E207 camera; 16:38:58.798 GMT), at about 305 degrees circumference.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 20
excerpt: This first very small flame was detected on image enhanced film at 58.788 seconds into the flight. It appeared to originate at about 305 degrees around the booster circumference at or near the aft field joint.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 58.788 s.

statement: The flame became a continuous, well-defined plume at 59.262 s; at about 60 s telemetry showed right SRB chamber pressure lower than the left.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 20
excerpt: It grew into a continuous, well-defined plume at 59.262 seconds. At about the same time (60 seconds), telemetry showed a pressure differential between the chamber pressures in the right and left boosters.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 59.262 s.

statement: The first visual indication that flame breached the External Tank was at 64.660 s MET (abrupt plume shape/color change indicating leaking hydrogen).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 20
excerpt: The first visual indication that swirling flame from the right Solid Rocket Booster breached the External Tank was at 64.660 seconds when there was an abrupt change in the shape and color of the plume.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 64.660 s.

statement: At 73.124 s MET a circumferential white vapor pattern on the External Tank aft dome marked the beginning of hydrogen tank structural failure.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 21
excerpt: At 73.124 seconds, a circumferential white vapor pattern was observed blooming from the side of the External Tank bottom dome. This was the beginning of the structural failure of the hydrogen tank that culminated in the entire aft dome dropping away.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 73.124 s.

statement: The intertank and lower liquid oxygen tank structures failed at 73.137 s MET.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 21
excerpt: These structures failed at 73.137 seconds as evidenced by the white vapors appearing in the intertank region.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. MET 73.137 s.

statement: The last validated Orbiter telemetry measurement was at 73.618 s MET (16:39:13.628 GMT).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, p. 19
excerpt: The last telemetry data from the Challenger was received 73.618 seconds after launch.
timeBasis: Source table "STS 51-L Sequence of Major Events" gives the event in GMT (hr:min:sec) on 1986-01-28; used directly as UTC. Row "Last validated Orbiter telemetry measurement" (V46P0120A); a last RF signal is listed at 74.130 s.

statement: Commission consensus: the loss was caused by a failure in the joint between the two lower segments of the right Solid Rocket Motor, specifically destruction of the seals meant to prevent hot gas leakage.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 40
excerpt: the loss of the Space Shuttle Challenger was caused by a failure in the joint between the two lower segments of the right Solid Rocket Motor. The specific failure was the destruction of the seals that are intended to prevent hot gases from leaking through the joint

statement: Conclusion: the cause was the failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Motor.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 72, Conclusion
excerpt: the Commission concluded that the cause of the Challenger accident was the failure of the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Motor.

statement: Conclusion: the failure was due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to temperature, physical dimensions, character of materials, reusability, processing, and joint reaction to dynamic loading.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 72, Conclusion
excerpt: The failure was due to a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to a number of factors. These factors were the effects of temperature, physical dimensions, the character of materials, the effects of reusability, processing, and the reaction of the joint to dynamic loading.
notes: Wording lists "character of materials" and "reaction of the joint to dynamic loading" (not "joint rotation").

statement: Finding 1: a combustion gas leak through the right SRM aft field joint, initiated at or shortly after ignition, weakened and/or penetrated the External Tank, initiating breakup.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 1
excerpt: A combustion gas leak through the right Solid Rocket Motor aft field joint initiated at or shortly after ignition eventually weakened and/or penetrated the External Tank initiating vehicle structural breakup

statement: Finding 2: no other 51-L element or the payload contributed to the joint leak; sabotage was not a factor.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 2
excerpt: The evidence shows that no other STS 51-L Shuttle element or the payload contributed to the causes of the right Solid Rocket Motor aft field joint combustion gas leak. Sabotage was not a factor.

statement: Finding 5: segments had grown in diameter from prior use; at launch the maximum tang-to-clevis gap at the O-rings was no more than .008 in and the average .004 in.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 5b-5c
excerpt: The diameters of the two Solid Rocket Motor segments had grown as a result of prior use. c. The growth resulted in a condition at time of launch wherein the maximum gap between the tang and clevis in the region of the joint's O-rings was no more than .008 inches

statement: Finding 6a: temperature at the 300-degree position on the right aft field joint was estimated at 28 +/- 5 degrees F, the coldest point on the joint; the sun-facing side was about 50 degrees F.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 6a-6b
excerpt: The temperature at the 300 degree position on the right aft field joint circumference was estimated to be 28degrees +/- 5 degrees Fahrenheit. This was the coldest point on the joint.
notes: Analytical estimate (thermal model), not a direct measurement.

statement: Finding 9b: a compressed O-ring at 75 degrees F is five times more responsive in returning to shape than one at 30 degrees F.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 71, Findings 9b
excerpt: A compressed O-ring at 75 degrees Fahrenheit is five times more responsive in returning to its uncompressed shape than a cold O-ring at 30 degrees Fahrenheit.

statement: Finding 10c: at the cold launch temperature the O-ring would probably not be pressure-actuated to seal in time to preclude blow-by and erosion.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 71, Findings 10c
excerpt: Thus, it is probable the O-ring would not be pressure actuated to seal the gap in time to preclude joint failure due to blow-by and erosion from hot combustion gases.

statement: Sub-scale dynamic tests: with a 0.004-inch initial gap, sealing without blow-by did not occur consistently until 55 degrees F.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 61, "O-Ring Compression at Launch (Static)"
excerpt: For the 0.004-inch initial gap condition, sealing without any gas blow-by, did not occur consistently until the temperature was raised to 55 degrees Fahrenheit.

statement: Finding 12: of 21 launches at 61 degrees F or above only four showed O-ring thermal distress; every launch below 61 degrees F showed distress in one or more O-rings.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 71, Findings 12
excerpt: Of 21 launches with ambient temperatures of 61 degrees Fahrenheit or greater, only four showed signs of O-ring thermal distress; i.e., erosion or blow-by and soot. Each of the launches below 61. degrees Fahrenheit resulted in one or more O-rings showing signs of thermal distress.

statement: Finding 13: water may have been in the 51-L clevis; it was cold enough to freeze, and tests show ice can inhibit secondary seal performance.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 71, Findings 13
excerpt: At time of launch, it was cold enough that water present in the joint would freeze. Tests show that ice in the joint can inhibit proper secondary seal performance.
notes: Stated as a possibility, not an established fact.

statement: Finding 16: the leak was again evident as flame at about 58 s; flame position centered at 307 degrees was confirmed by two recovered right SRB fragments; the joint may have been temporarily resealed by aluminum oxide deposits (alternative).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 72, Findings 16, 16b
excerpt: Alternatively, the O-ring gap could have been resealed by deposition of a fragile buildup of aluminum oxide and other combustion debris.
notes: Commission presents two alternatives (16a continuous small leak; 16b temporary reseal) without choosing between them.

statement: Ch. V opening finding: the decision to launch was flawed; decision makers were unaware of the O-ring problem history, the contractor's initial written recommendation against launch below 53 degrees F, and continuing Thiokol engineer opposition.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 82
excerpt: The decision to launch the Challenger was flawed. Those who made that decision were unaware of the recent history of problems concerning the O-rings and the joint and were unaware of the initial written recommendation of the contractor advising against the launch at temperatures below 53 degrees Fahrenheit

statement: Commission judgment: had decision makers known all the facts it is highly unlikely they would have launched on 28 January 1986.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 82
excerpt: If the decisionmakers had known all of the facts, it is highly unlikely that they would have decided to launch 51-L on January 28, 1986.

statement: Neither the July 1985 launch constraint, its reason, nor six consecutive waivers before 51-L were known to Moore (Level I), Aldrich (Level II) or Thomas.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 84
excerpt: Neither the launch constraint, the reason for it, or the six consecutive waivers prior to 51-L were known to Moore (Level I) or Aldrich (Level II) or Thomas at the time of the Flight Readiness Review process for 51-L.

statement: The Mission Management Team scrubbed the 27 January launch at 12:36 p.m. due to high cross winds; the following discussion produced no SRB constraints for a 9:38 a.m. launch on 28 January.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 85
excerpt: At 12:36 p.m. on the 27th, the Mission Management Team scrubbed the launch for that day due to high cross winds at the launch site.
timeBasis: Source gives 12:36 p.m. on 27 January; chronology table marks it EST (UTC-5); converted to UTC.

statement: The first phase of the Marshall-Thiokol teleconference began at 5:45 p.m. EST on 27 January. The Commission narrative says Thiokol presented low-temperature concerns "along with an opinion that launch should be delayed"; this point is contested in testimony (CH-C085).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 87
excerpt: The first phase of the teleconference began at 5:45 p. m. Eastern Standard Time; participants included Reinartz, Lovingood, Hardy, and numerous people at Kennedy, Marshall and Thiokol-Wasatch.
timeBasis: Source gives Eastern Standard Time (EST = UTC-5); converted to UTC.

statement: Phase 2 of the teleconference commenced at approximately 8:45 p.m. EST after Thiokol charts arrived by telefax.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 88
excerpt: At approximately 8:45 p.m. Eastern Standard Time, Phase 2 of the teleconference commenced, the Thiokol charts and written data having arrived at Kennedy Space Center by telefax.
timeBasis: Source gives an approximate Eastern Standard Time (EST = UTC-5); converted to UTC; precision is approximate.

statement: Chronology: Thiokol (Lund) recommended not flying 51-L until O-ring temperature reached 53 degrees F, the lowest of any previous flight; Kilminster said he could not recommend launch.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 107, Chronology, "Approximately 8:45 PM (EST)" entry
excerpt: Recommendation by Thiokol (Lund) is not to fly STS 51-L (SAM-25) until the temperature of the O-ring reached 53 degrees Fahrenheit, which was the lowest temperature of any previous flight.
notes: Commission reconstruction (post-accident chronology, 1986), not a record made at the time. The Lund conclusions chart itself is reproduced only as an image in the HTML; content here is from the Commission chronology and testimony.

statement: Kilminster requested a five-minute off-net caucus that lasted about 30 minutes; the teleconference recessed at about 10:30 p.m. EST.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 92
excerpt: At that time Joe Kilminster requested a five minute off-net caucus, and that caucus lasted approximately 30 minutes. The teleconference was recessed at approximately 10:30 p.m. Eastern Standard Time.
timeBasis: Source gives an approximate Eastern Standard Time (EST = UTC-5); converted to UTC; precision is approximate.

statement: Boisjoly testified that Mason opened the caucus saying a management decision was necessary and asked Lund to take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, pp. 92-93 (Boisjoly testimony, Hearing Transcript Feb 25, 1986, pp. 1418-1422)
excerpt: He turned to Bob Lund and asked him to take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat.

statement: Chronology: final management review by Mason, Lund, Kilminster and Wiggins; final agreement cited erosion margin of three times the previous worst case and the secondary O-ring being in position.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 108, Chronology, "Approximately 10:30 PM (EST)" entry
excerpt: Final agreement is: (1) there is a substantial margin to erode the primary O-ring by a factor of three times the previous worst case, and (2) even if the primary O-ring does not seal, the secondary is in position and will.
notes: Commission reconstruction (post-accident chronology, 1986), not a record made at the time.

statement: At about 11 p.m. EST the teleconference resumed; Thiokol management said temperature effects were a concern but data inconclusive, and Kilminster read the rationale recommending launch.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 96
excerpt: At approximately 11 p.m. Eastern Standard Time, the Thiokol/NASA teleconference resumed, the Thiokol management stating that they had reassessed the problem, that the temperature effects were a concern, but that the data were admittedly inconclusive.
timeBasis: Source gives an approximate Eastern Standard Time (EST = UTC-5); converted to UTC; precision is approximate.

statement: Hardy requested the Thiokol recommendation in writing by telefax to Kennedy and Marshall, and it was sent; the chronology places a Kilminster-signed fax at about 11:45 p.m. EST.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 96; Chronology "Approximately 11:45 PM (EST) Telefax"
excerpt: Hardy requested that it be sent in writing by telefax both to Kennedy and to Marshall, and it was.
timeBasis: Chronology entry heading "Approximately 11:45 PM (EST)"; converted EST (UTC-5) to UTC. Entry text in the HTML transcription is garbled ("9:45 M EST, 27 January 1986 ( 11 :45 EST"), likely 9:45 p.m. MST = 11:45 p.m. EST.
notes: The telefax (Figure 5.4) is reproduced as an image only; its text was not verified from the HTML.

statement: Commission Finding 4 (Ch. V): Thiokol management reversed its position and recommended launch at the urging of Marshall and contrary to its engineers, to accommodate a major customer.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 104, Findings 4
excerpt: The Commission concluded that the Thiokol Management reversed its position and recommended the launch of 51-L, at the urging of Marshall and contrary to the views of its engineers in order to accommodate a major customer.

statement: Commission Finding 1 (Ch. V): there was a serious flaw in the decision making process; a well-structured safety system would have flagged the rising doubts about the joint seal.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 104, Findings 1
excerpt: The Commission concluded that there was a serious flaw in the decision making process leading up to the launch of flight 51-L. A well structured and managed system emphasizing safety would have flagged the rising doubts about the Solid Rocket Booster joint seal.

statement: Commission Finding 2 (Ch. V): waiving of launch constraints appears to have been at the expense of flight safety.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 104, Findings 2
excerpt: The waiving of launch constraints appears to have been at the expense of flight safety. There was no system which made it imperative that launch constraints and waivers of launch constraints be considered by all levels of management.

statement: Commission Finding 3 (Ch. V): Marshall management showed a propensity to contain potentially serious problems internally rather than communicate them forward.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 104, Findings 3
excerpt: The Commission is troubled by what appears to be a propensity of management at Marshall to contain potentially serious problems and to attempt to resolve them internally rather than communicate them forward.

statement: Reinartz testified that he made the decision not to escalate the issue to Level II.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 88 (Hearing Transcript Feb 26, 1986)
excerpt: Mr. Hotz: Mr. Reinartz, are you telling us that you in fact are the person who made the decision not to escalate this to a Level II item? Mr. Reinartz: That is correct, sir.

statement: Smith, Thomas, Aldrich and Moore each testified they did not know before launch of Thiokol's objections.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 103 (Hearing Transcript Feb 27, 1986, p. 1899)
excerpt: Mr. Smith [Kennedy Space Center Director]: I did not. Mr. Thomas [Launch Director]: No, sir. Mr. Aldrich [Shuttle Program Director]: I did not. Mr. Moore [Associate Administrator for Space Flight]: I did not.

statement: Mulloy testified that in the ~11:30 p.m. call to Aldrich about recovery-area weather he did not discuss the Thiokol conversations, regarding it as a resolved Level III issue.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 98 (Mulloy testimony)
excerpt: I did not discuss with Mr. Aldrich the conversations that we had just completed with Morton Thiokol.
timeBasis: Mulloy testimony: "at about 11:30 p.m." on 27 Jan; EST assumed from the chronology (UTC-5); approximate.

statement: At about 5:00 a.m. on 28 January Mulloy told Lucas only that Thiokol temperature concerns had been resolved in favor of launch.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 100
excerpt: At about 5:00 a. m . on January 28, a discussion took place among Messrs. Mulloy, Lucas, and Reinartz in which Mulloy reported to Lucas only that there had been a discussion with Thiokol over their concerns about temperature effects on the O-rings
timeBasis: Source gives about 5:00 a.m. at Kennedy; chronology table is EST (UTC-5); approximate.

statement: Ice crew infrared pyrometer readings (7:00-9:00 a.m. EST) showed the left SRB at about 25 degrees F and the right SRB at about 8 degrees F near the aft region; not reported since no LCC covered surface temperatures.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 110, Chronology "Approximately 7:00-9:00 AM (EST)"
excerpt: Left-hand SRB appears to be about 25 degrees F. and right-hand SRB appears to be about 8 degrees F. near the aft region. Ice crew is not concerned since there is no Launch Commit Criteria on surface temperatures and does not report.
notes: Commission reconstruction (post-accident chronology, 1986), not a record made at the time. Point surface readings by hand pyrometer; reliability not assessed in this chapter.

statement: Ice finding 1: Rockwell's launch recommendation was ambiguous; the Commission found it difficult to conclude there was a no-launch recommendation.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 117, ice Findings 1
excerpt: An analysis of all of the testimony and interviews establishes that Rockwell's recommendation on launch was ambiguous. The Commission finds it difficult, as did Mr. Aldrich, to conclude that there was a no-launch recommendation.

statement: Ice finding 2: the ice was not a cause of the accident, though the decision to launch was questionable; NASA appeared to require the contractor to prove it was unsafe.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 118, ice Findings 2
excerpt: Nevertheless, the Commission has determined that the ice was not a cause of the 51-L accident and does not conclude that NASA's decision to launch specifically overrode a no-launch recommendation by an element contractor.

statement: Ice finding 3: the pad 39B freeze protection plan was inadequate and margins of safety were whittled down too far.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. V, p. 118, ice Findings 3
excerpt: The Commission believes that the severe cold and presence of so much ice on the fixed service structure made it inadvisable to launch on the morning of January 28, and that margins of safety were whittled down too far.

statement: The SRB problem began with faulty joint design; NASA and Thiokol failed to recognize it, then failed to fix it, and finally treated it as an acceptable flight risk.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 120
excerpt: The Space Shuttle's Solid Rocket Booster problem began with the faulty design of its joint and increased as both NASA and contractor management first failed to recognize it as a problem, then failed to fix it and finally treated it as an acceptable flight risk.

statement: STS 51-C (24 January 1985) had O-ring temperature of 53 degrees F, the coldest to that date; erosion occurred in both boosters and for the first time a secondary O-ring showed heat effect.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 134-135, "STS 51-C and Cold Temperature"
excerpt: This was also the first flight where a secondary O-ring showed the effect of heat.
notes: Text: "The temperature of the O-rings at launch was 53.... degrees, the coldest to that date" (split across a figure).

statement: At the Level I FRR for 51-E (21 Feb 1985) the issue was resolved as "acceptable risk because of limited exposure and redundancy".
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 147
excerpt: the previous 18-page analysis had been reduced to a one page chart with the resolution: "acceptable risk because of limited exposure and redundancy (Ref. STS 41-C FRR)". 152 No mention of temperature was found in the Level I report.

statement: STS 51-B (29 April 1985) nozzle primary O-ring failed to seal; .171 in of erosion far exceeded the .070 in maximum predicted by a recent model.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 147
excerpt: There was no mention of the fact that .171 inches of erosion on the primary O-ring far exceeded a more recent analysis model prediction of .070 inches maximum possible erosion.

statement: Boisjoly's 31 July 1985 memo to Lund ("O-ring Erosion/Potential Failure Criticality") warned a field-joint failure would be a catastrophe of the highest order.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 139 (Boisjoly memorandum, 31 July 1985, as quoted by the Commission)
excerpt: If the same scenario should occur in a field joint (and it could), then it is a jump ball whether as to the success or failure of the joint because the secondary O-ring cannot respond to the clevis opening rate and may not be capable of pressurization.
notes: Memo text verified only as quoted in Ch. VI; the original memo was not separately retrieved.

statement: Managers on 27 January compared only flights with O-ring distress against temperature, not all flights; including all flights shows all four flights at 63 degrees F or below had distress versus three of twenty at 66 degrees F or above.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 145-146, "Temperature Effects", Figures 6-7
excerpt: This comparison of flight history indicates that only three incidents of O-ring thermal distress occurred out of twenty flights with O-ring temperatures at 66 degrees Fahrenheit or above, whereas, all four flights with O-ring temperatures at 63 degrees Fahrenheit or below experienced O-ring thermal distress.
notes: Thresholds here (63/66 F joint temperatures) differ from Ch. IV Finding 12 (61 F ambient, 21 launches).

statement: Ch. VI finding 3: NASA and Thiokol accepted escalating risk apparently because they "got away with it last time" (Feynman: "a kind of Russian roulette").
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 148, Findings 3
excerpt: NASA and Thiokol accepted escalating risk apparently because they "got away with it last time." As Commissioner Feynman observed, the decision making was: "a kind of Russian roulette.

statement: Ch. VI finding 1: the joint test and certification program was inadequate (qualification motors not configured as in flight; tested horizontally).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 148, Findings 1
excerpt: The joint test and certification program was inadequate. There was no requirement to configure the qualifications test motor as it would be in flight, and the motors were static tested in a horizontal position, not in the vertical flight position.

statement: No safety, reliability or quality assurance representative was invited to the 27 January teleconference or sat on the Mission Management Team.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VII, p. 152
excerpt: No one thought to invite a safety representative or a reliability and quality assurance engineer to the January 27, 1986, teleconference between Marshall and Thiokol.

statement: Ch. VII finding 4: little or no trend analysis was performed on O-ring erosion and blow-by.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VII, p. 161, Findings 4
excerpt: Little or no trend analysis was performed on O-ring erosion and blow-by problems.

statement: Ch. VIII finding 4: the scheduled flight rate did not reflect capabilities and resources; there was no margin for unforeseen hardware problems.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VIII, Findings 4 (p. 177)
excerpt: The scheduled flight rate did not accurately reflect the capabilities and resources.

statement: Commission Recommendation I - Design: the faulty SRM joint and seal must be changed; joints must be fully understood, tested and verified; NRC independent oversight committee.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation I, p. 198
excerpt: The faulty Solid Rocket Motor joint and seal must be changed. This could be a new design eliminating the joint or a redesign of the current joint and seal.

statement: Commission Recommendation II - Shuttle Management Structure: review the program structure, give the Program Manager authority; astronauts in management; STS Safety Advisory Panel.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation II, p. 199
excerpt: The Shuttle Program Structure should be reviewed. The project managers for the various elements of the Shuttle program felt more accountable to their center management than to the Shuttle program organization.

statement: Commission Recommendation III - Criticality Review and Hazard Analysis: review all Criticality 1, 1R, 2 and 2R items and hazard analyses, with an NRC audit panel.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation III, p. 199
excerpt: NASA and the primary Shuttle contractors should review all Criticality 1, 1R, 2, and 2R items and hazard analyses.

statement: Commission Recommendation IV - Safety Organization: establish an Office of Safety, Reliability and Quality Assurance under an Associate Administrator reporting directly to the Administrator.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation IV, p. 199
excerpt: NASA should establish an Office of Safety, Reliability and Quality Assurance to be headed by an Associate administrator, reporting directly to the NASA Administrator.

statement: Commission Recommendation V - Improved Communications: eliminate Marshall management isolation; a policy on launch constraints; record FRRs and MMT meetings; crew commander attends FRR.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation V, p. 200
excerpt: A policy should be developed which governs the imposition and removal of Shuttle launch constraints. Flight Readiness Reviews and Mission Management Team meetings should be recorded.

statement: Commission Recommendation VI - Landing Safety: improve tire, brake and nosewheel steering; criteria for Kennedy landings.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation VI, p. 200
excerpt: NASA must take actions to improve landing safety. The tire, brake and nosewheel steering systems must be improved.

statement: Commission Recommendation VII - Launch Abort and Crew Escape: crew escape during controlled gliding flight; extend emergency runway landing conditions.
locator: Vol. I, Recommendations, Recommendation VII, p. 200
excerpt: Make all efforts to provide a crew escape system for use during controlled gliding flight.

statement: Commission Recommendation VIII - Flight Rate: establish a flight rate consistent with resources; avoid reliance on a single launch capability; firm payload assignment policy.

notes: Narrative time is approximate ("about").

statement: The range safety system destructed the right SRB at 110.250 s MET (39:50.260 GMT) and the left at 110.252 s.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. III, pp. 37-39, event table rows "RH SRB RSS destruct" / "LH SRB RSS destruct"
excerpt: 39:50.260 RH SRB RSS destruct 110.250 E202 Camera
timeBasis: Source table gives GMT; used directly as UTC.

statement: Finding 8b: the External Tank-SRB strut at 310 degrees, near the failed aft field joint, enhances tang-clevis gap opening by about 10-20 percent at 300-320 degrees.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 8b
excerpt: This strut's effect on the joint dynamics is to enhance the opening of the gap between the tang and clevis by about 10-20 percent in the region of 300-320 degrees.
notes: Co-factor locating the failure near 300 degrees (CH-R03).

statement: Finding 11c: putty-related delay in pressure application could be a factor in initial joint failure (stated as possibility).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 71, Findings 11b-11c
excerpt: This delay in pressure could be a factor in initial joint failure.
notes: Plausible, not established co-factor (CH-R03). Finding 11b gives delays of 500 ms or more.

statement: Finding 7: other joints on both SRBs had similar combinations of tang-clevis gap and temperature; whether they were distressed in flight is unknown.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 7
excerpt: Other joints on the left and right Solid Rocket Boosters experienced similar combinations of tang-to-clevis gap clearance and temperature. It is not known whether these joints experienced distress during the flight of 51-L.
notes: Indicates cold plus gap does not alone explain why this joint failed (CH-R03).

statement: Finding 6b: the side of the right SRB facing the sun was estimated at about 50 degrees F, versus 28 +/- 5 F at the 300-degree point.
locator: Vol. I, Ch. IV, p. 70, Findings 6b
excerpt: Temperature on the opposite side of the right Solid Rocket Booster facing the sun was estimated to be about 50 degrees Fahrenheit.
notes: Analytical estimate; shows the large circumferential gradient (compare CH-C020).

statement: CAIB (2003, later knowledge): the Flight Readiness Review process was altered after Challenger, but the changes did not erase the basic problems built into its structure.
locator: CAIB Report Vol. I, Ch. 8, p. 198 (printed page inferred: chapter PDF p. 4, between printed pp. 197 and 199)
excerpt: Although the process was altered after Challenger, these changes did not erase the basic problems that were built into the structure of the Flight Readiness Review.
notes: Later analysis (2003) with respect to Challenger; CAIB is a primary investigation report for Columbia. Used here only as later knowledge on whether the post-Challenger organizational changes were effective, not to judge what 1986-88 actors knew. Bears on Recommendation V / launch-decision changes (CH-C076, CH-C079). Printed page number not legible in the text layer; inferred from adjacent pages.

statement: The 19 August 1985 Thiokol/Marshall briefing to NASA Headquarters concluded it was safe to continue flying the existing design provided all joints were leak checked at 200 psig, free of contamination and met squeeze requirements (Figure 5 conclusions).
locator: Vol. I, Ch. VI, p. 140 (text quoting the briefing; Figure 5 on p. 139)
excerpt: it is safe to continue flying existing design as long as all joints are leak checked with a 200 psig stabilization pressure, are free of contamination in the seal areas and meet O-ring squeeze requirements.
notes: Contemporary briefing (1985) as quoted by the Commission; the briefing document itself was not retrieved.
